Learning Objectives
Understand the role of rehabilitation in the treatment of patients with intra-articular hip
conditions.
Summarize common movement impairments in patients with intra-articular hip conditions.
Recognize the key components of postoperative rehabilitation for patients with intra-articular
hip conditions.
Appraise the quality of a nonsurgical or postoperative rehabilitation program for patients with
intra-articular hip conditions.

Rehabilitation is important in patients with hip-related groin pain. Hip-related groin pain is
pain in the anterior hip and/or groin region from the hip joint itself. This pain also is referred to
as intra-articular pathology and includes the following:
Femoroacetabular impingement (FAI)
Acetabular dysplasia
Acetabular labral tears
Pain in the groin region that is not hip related may be from structures such as the inguinal
canal, pubic symphysis, or adductors or iliopsoas muscles.1
Physical Therapists are Experts in the Movement System

Physical Therapists are Experts in the Movement System
The movement system is “the integration of body systems that generate and maintain
movement at all levels of bodily function.”2 Human movement is a complex interaction
between environment, task, and individual. Therefore, a physical therapist’s expertise is
in observing how an individual patient moves during functional tasks and activities to
understand if and how the individual’s movement patterns, morphology, strength, and
flexibility contribute to the current presentation and pain pattern.
Physical Therapy Evaluation to Individualize Treatment

Physical Therapy Evaluation to Individualize Treatment
Via a thorough evaluation, the physical therapist detects impairments in neuromuscular
control, strength, and flexibility to investigate an individual’s unique functional
limitations and pain patterns. The evaluation includes assessment of body positions and
movement patterns while monitoring a patient’s symptoms. Modification of symptoms
by changing positions and movement patterns directly informs management. Although
changes in positions and movements are noted by observing joint angles, these changes
affect underlying joint tissue loads. The change in tissue load likely is important. Based
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:23 PM
AAOS | Hip Rehabilitation
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000532
2/31

on a fundamental understanding of body structure and biomechanical principles,
physical therapists design individualized treatment options to manage observed
movement impairments, with a focus on returning patients to their prior or desired
levels of activity. Although patient-specific morphology is considered during the physical
therapy evaluation, morphology does not determine management.
Morphology and Movement Dysfunction

Morphology and Movement Dysfunction
Often, the presumption is that all patients with the same diagnosis have similar
movement patterns and functional limitations and, therefore, may benefit from the
same rehabilitation program; however, greater variability exists within each medical
diagnosis and many common features are present between diagnoses. Although
evidence supporting movement impairments based on hip joint morphology is reviewed,
high-quality rehabilitation is patient specific rather than pathology specific. Most studies
to date are small, cross-sectional studies; therefore, knowledge of contributors to pain
and dysfunction is limited. By appreciating an individual’s movement patterns and their
underlying morphology, physical therapists can discern the role that altered movement
may play in the generation of pain and pathology and the resolution of pain and return
to function.
Morphology-Specific Movement Impairments During Functional Tasks
Based on current evidence, several movement impairments are commonly noted in patients
with hip-related groin pain.
Femoroacetabular Impingement
Walking
Multiple studies of walking note differences between patients with FAI and individuals without
hip pain, including the following3-6:
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:23 PM
AAOS | Hip Rehabilitation
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000532
3/31

Decreased hip and pelvic excursion in the frontal plane
Decreased peak hip extension and internal rotation angle
Decreased peak hip abduction during swing phase
Bilateral Squat
This movement involves end-range hip flexion and has been suggested as a screening tool for
FAI; however, the bilateral squat is performed on both legs and, therefore, requires minimal
control in the frontal or transverse planes. Differences noted between patients with FAI and
individuals without hip pain include the following7-9:
Reduced squat depth and speed
Decreased sagittal plane pelvic excursion, increased anterior pelvic tilt and hip adduction;
this movement pattern may result in earlier impingement.
Single-leg Tasks
Dissimilar from bilateral tasks, single-leg tasks require control in multiple planes of movement
and at a higher load level. Despite the importance of multiplanar control, the literature is
sparse. Movement pattern differences include the following10-13:
Patients with FAI perform a single-leg step down with greater hip flexion and anterior pelvic
tilt than individuals without hip pain; these are positions that may contribute to
impingement.
Patients with FAI perform a single-leg squat with less hip adduction than individuals without
hip pain.
Patients with hip-related groin pain perform a single-leg squat with less hip flexion and less
knee flexion and squat to a reduced depth compared with individuals without hip pain.
Compared with the asymptomatic limb, the symptomatic limb of patients with unilateral hip-
related groin pain has less total sagittal plane range of motion than during a single-leg drop
jump.
Stair Climbing
Ascending and descending stairs is a common functional task requiring hip strength and
control in multiple planes. Movement differences in patients with FAI compared with
individuals without hip pain include the following:
Reduced sagittal plane range of motion, primarily because of decreased hip extension14

Increased transverse plane pelvic range of motion and maximum anterior pelvic tilt14
Increased forward trunk flexion15
Participants

Participants
Most of the evidence on movement impairments in FAI is from male participants;
females comprise approximately 25% of the total research sample. More recently,
studies including female participants and assessing sex-specific differences have become
more common. These studies suggest movement pattern differences between females
and males with FAI; however, additional research is necessary to determine the sex-
specific differences.5,16
Acetabular Dysplasia
Most research in this area is in adolescents or adults with mild to moderate dysplasia from
small studies with a wide age range.17-20
Walking
Differences in movement patterns between patients with dysplasia and individuals without
dysplasia include the following:
Decreased sagittal plane hip excursion and peak hip extension compared with individuals
without hip pain
Increased hip adduction and external rotation angle may be present.
Decreased peak hip flexion angle (patients with severe dysplasia); increased peak hip flexion
angle (patients with less severe dysplasia)
Decreased hip extension and increased hip adduction and pelvic drop on the painful side
compared with the asymptomatic side
Common Movement Impairments in Hip-Related Groin Pain
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:23 PM


Common Movement Impairments in Hip-Related Groin Pain
A common feature across multiple patient populations with hip-related groin pain is
decreased hip extension during gait. This movement impairment also is noted in
patients with hip osteoarthritis. Therefore, whether this impairment is because of pain,
morphology, or early arthritic changes is unclear. Another common feature is increased
hip adduction. This is observed in females with FAI and patients with acetabular
dysplasia. Because dysplasia is more common in females than males, interpretation of
these differences is unclear.
Focus on Walking

Focus on Walking
The most common functional activity investigated is walking; however, walking does not
require end-range hip motion or maximal strength. Observation of walking alone may
not be sufficient to elucidate movement impairments that contribute to a patient’s
symptoms. Higher level activities should be observed, including sport-specific
movements, to fully recognize the limitations present in patients with hip-related groin
pain.
The Role of Physical Therapy

The Role of Physical Therapy
Although most studies show small, but detectable differences between patients with hip-
related groin pain and individuals without hip pain, whether these movement
differences are related to the pain, the morphology, muscle strength, or something else
is unclear. Whether these movement differences are positively adaptive (ie, they reduce
pain or dysfunction) or maladaptive (ie, they contribute to pain and dysfunction) also is
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:23 PM
AAOS | Hip Rehabilitation
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000532
6/31

unclear. Some evidence suggests that morphology is not the primary driver of
movement impairment. For example, the severity of FAI morphology (ie, the alpha angle
of the cam morphology) does not appear to be related to the movement pattern
observed.21 In addition, surgical management of the underlying morphology results in
minimal changes in the observed movement patterns during walking, bilateral squat,
and stair climbing.14,22-24
The limited group of published rehabilitation intervention studies has shown that
rehabilitation may improve self-reported function in patients with intra-articular hip
conditions.25-30 Early evidence from the only two trials that include movement retraining
as part of management shows that changing movement patterns may reduce symptoms
and improve function.28,30 For example, in patients with hip-related groin pain, reducing
hip adduction motion during functional tasks was associated with improvements in pain
and function.29 A mechanical interpretation of the interaction of movement and
morphology suggests that movement impairments may contribute to hip pain and
dysfunction. For example, increased anterior pelvic tilt is commonly noted during
functional tasks in patients with FAI. This position would result in impingement earlier
during range of motion than if the pelvis were in a neutral position.31 Therefore, a
patient’s movement patterns may accentuate the effect of rather than accommodate for
altered morphology. Physical therapy to provide individualized rehabilitation, informed
by a thorough evaluation with an emphasis on precise and controlled movement, is
recommended as a first-line treatment option for individuals with hip-related groin pain.
Key Examination Components to Inform Rehabilitation

Key Examination Components to Inform Rehabilitation
Intra-articular hip conditions, such as acetabular labral tears, acetabular dysplasia, and
FAI, often present as anteromedial hip and groin pain across a wide range of functional
activities. For example, a patient may report pain with sleeping, prolonged standing, and
walking more than 10 minutes, whereas another patient may report pain with deep
squatting and high-flexion sports activities (ie, hockey). These pain patterns may be
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:23 PM
AAOS | Hip Rehabilitation
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000532
7/31

unique to each patient and their functional demands and, therefore, necessitate
position- and activity-specific assessment. Key elements of the subjective and objective
examination are important in guiding nonsurgical, preoperative, and postoperative
treatment of patients with intra-articular hip conditions.
In addition to questions on the history of the condition (eg, duration of symptoms,
mechanism of injury, initial symptoms), the subjective history should include questions
about the patient’s physical activity patterns and participation. This information should
include but may not be limited to activity demands (ie, cutting/pivoting, deep squatting,
flexibility), context (ie, work, recreational, competitive sports activities), exposure (ie,
frequency, intensity, time), and desired or expected level of activity after treatment.
Assessment of body positions and movement patterns is important in determining if and
how pain is associated with the manner in which a patient is performing various
activities. The goal of this approach is to identify the patient’s preferred movement
patterns and determine if changing these patterns may modify the symptoms. Postures
and movement patterns that deviate considerably from optimal alignment may place
increased external loads on the hip and require increased balancing torques from the
supporting muscles. Specifically, if optimizing a patient’s biomechanics reduces pain
during the examination, then rehabilitation, including posture and movement training, is
advised. A portion of the examination should precede standard, examination table-
based special tests to avoid irritating the patient’s joint, which may increase the
likelihood of false-positive findings during this dynamic assessment. The findings from
this portion of the examination should then directly inform subsequent assessment of
range of motion, flexibility, and strength.
Available evidence on common biomechanical findings in patients with intra-articular
conditions is focused primarily on patients with FAI.3 Based on the available literature
and clinical experience, the authors of this lesson have identified methods to modify
symptoms via adjustments to posture and movement patterns3,5,10,12,32-35 (Table 1).
Response to symptom modification (ie, reduced hip pain with optimal posture) may
directly inform the components of rehabilitation (ie, postural training and education).

Response to rehabilitation often is used to determine appropriate surgical treatment for
patients with intra-articular hip conditions. General guidelines for reassessment include
the following:
Reassessment can be used to evaluate within-session management effects (eg,
change in posture, body mechanics, manual therapy).32
Reassessment should be performed at a minimum of 12 weeks to determine the
optimal response to rehabilitation.
Randomized trials have reported varied duration and frequency of physical therapy,
ranging from 6 to 12 visits between 6 and 24 weeks.25-27
Improvement may occur much earlier than 12 weeks. Observation of pain reduction
within the session,32 neuromuscular improvements (ie, improvements in posture
and control of movement) within the first 4 weeks, and strength improvements
within 6 to 8 weeks is possible.
Patients with painful joints may take longer to respond to strength training.
If pain and/or other symptoms are worsening in response to or despite
management and cannot be attributed to other factors, reassessment should occur
earlier.
The authors of this lesson also suggest using the following questions to assess the
components of a good rehabilitation program:
Are the patient’s symptomatic activities being managed via targeted posture and
movement assessments and interventions?
Are the patient’s symptoms from immediate and sustained responses being used to
modify the program?
Is the patient being monitored via criterion-based progression using acceptable
measures/tools?
Is the patient able to complete the home program? (ie, do some or all the activities re-
create their familiar pain?)
Does the program include education, advice, and monitoring with respect to return to
desired activity?

Nonsurgical Rehabilitation

Nonsurgical Rehabilitation
Rehabilitation for those seeking nonsurgical management of intra-articular hip
conditions should aim to reduce pain and optimize function to restore the patient’s
desired level of activity participation. Based on the examination findings and with
consideration of the patient’s goals, management should include patient education to
optimize posture and movement patterns and guidance on how to safely resume
physical activity. Management also should emphasize improved joint mobility, flexibility,
and strength as appropriate, with consideration of the patient’s structural anatomy.
Patients should receive thorough home exercise program instruction that is consistent
with and builds on the in-clinic program. This information should include explicit
instructions for the proper performance of each exercise, appropriate exercise dosage,
and activity parameters to integrate into daily routine. Advice to reduce or avoid physical
activity should be provided judiciously and with a clear understanding of the patient’s
pain patterns and potential contributing factors to avoid. A thorough examination, which
includes posture and movement assessment, aids clinicians in providing more precise
and effective rehabilitation and activity guidance.
The Physical Stress Theory, the concept that biologic tissues adapt predictability to
physical stress,43 is a reasonable model on which the management of intra-articular hip
conditions can be framed. Specifically, the Physical Stress Theory proposes that optimal
stress yields appropriate adaptation and that exceptionally low or very high stress
conditions may initiate negative biologic processes. This stress may be conferred
through patient-specific physiological factors (eg, age, systemic health conditions),
psychosocial factors (eg, mental health, social support), extrinsic factors (eg, footwear,
ergonomics) or movement factors (eg, muscle performance, motor control, physical
activity); each of these areas is likely to affect patients with intra-articular hip conditions.
The movement factors of the Physical Stress Theory, such as muscle weakness, altered
biomechanics, and reduced physical activity, often are associated with hip pain in
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:23 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000532

otherwise healthy adolescents and young adults. Therefore, an active intervention
approach in which exercise and education take precedent is advised. Passive treatment
approaches are unlikely to yield an effect if used in isolation or as the sole treatment
approach for individuals with intra-articular hip conditions. Modalities such as ice/heat,
ultrasonography, and transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation may provide
temporary pain relief but do not remediate weakness, joint motion/flexibility deficits, or
movement impairments. This movement-focused approach is not all-encompassing;
therefore, clinicians should consider other sources of stress that may be influencing a
patient’s pain and severity of disability.
Postoperative Rehabilitation

Postoperative Rehabilitation
Patients who have undergone surgical treatment for the management of intra-articular
hip conditions should participate in physical therapist–led postoperative rehabilitation;44
the potential benefits of participating in rehabilitation far outweigh the risks. Given the
various surgical hip procedures that can be performed, the physical therapist must have
specific knowledge of the surgical procedure performed and must be involved in the
development and implementation of guidelines to be followed during the postoperative
period.
The four phases of postoperative rehabilitation include the following:
Phase 1: early, protective phase
Phase 2: activities are progressed gradually; however, weight-bearing or range-of-
motion restrictions may remain in place to protect healing tissues.
Phase 3: prepares the patient for full return to daily activities
Phase4: for patients who wish to return to high-level sports activity
A criterion-based approach for patient progression through the phases is
recommended; therefore, a specific duration for each phase is not suggested. The
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:23 PM
AAOS | Hip Rehabilitation
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000532
16/31

duration varies based on the surgical procedure performed, the associated healing times
of the tissues involved, and the patient’s ability to meet phase criteria.
Many of the concepts described in the nonsurgical rehabilitation section should be
considered during postoperative rehabilitation. First, the patient’s daily activities should
be assessed to ensure that the patient can complete the tasks safely and that the tissues
affected by the initial injury and the surgical procedure are adequately protected. Patient
education should be provided to optimize alignment during static positions, such as
sitting and sleeping, and movement patterns during tasks, such as walking and stair
negotiation. Second, the patient should be educated on methods to gradually return to
previous activities in a manner that promotes tissue healing in the early phases and
tissue strengthening in the later phases. Third, the patient should be provided a home
exercise program to achieve optimal hip joint range of motion given the patient’s
structural anatomy; to improve hip muscle strength; to optimize cardiovascular fitness;
and to facilitate a return to full activities, including work, leisure, fitness, and sport, if
applicable.
Considerations for Surgical Management
Evidence suggests that some patients may improve with nonsurgical management.29,30,45,46
Consensus statements recommend 3 to 6 months of nonsurgical management before surgical
management.44,47
Presurgical instruction
Patients should be educated on what to expect postoperatively, including projected recovery
time, precautions to be followed, and potential need for assistance.
Equipment recommendations should be provided as necessary.
Crutches or another assistive device, if appropriate
Raised toilet seat
Tub bench with a handheld showerhead
Long-handled devices for reaching objects, putting on shoes, and bathing
Compressive stockings or device
Education on positioning and mobility
Daily tasks

Hip muscle strengthening, without increasing pain, such that the elevated pain persists the

General Principles
The physical therapist should be provided the specific diagnosis and description of the surgical
procedure to be aware of the specific tissues affected by the original injury and the surgical
procedure.
Current knowledge of tissue healing rates and factors that moderate healing (ie, age and
comorbidities) should be used to select and progress exercises and guide gradual return to
previous activity level.43
Progression of rehabilitation should be based on basic principles of tissue healing and patient
presentation (criterion-based rather than time-based).
Patients should be monitored closely for their response to treatment, and activities should be
progressed or regressed accordingly. If present, the magnitude and location of symptoms
should be determined during exercises and/or daily activity.
Patients should be educated to monitor their own symptoms and adjust their program
accordingly. For example, muscle soreness indicating an appropriate overloading during
strengthening activities is to be expected. A pinching sensation in the groin or a reproduction
of the patient’s primary preoperative complaint should be avoided.
Each patient’s structural morphology should be noted, and joint range of motion should be
progressed appropriately. Noting the amount of range of motion available at the hip and the
end feel of the motion is important. Excessive overpressure at the end of joint motion should
be avoided in the following circumstances:
A hard, bony end feel is detected, indicating bony anatomy that cannot be modified with
exercise.
The patient is demonstrating excessive motion at the joint. Additional overpressure may
contribute to micro-instability at the hip joint.
Patients should be encouraged to use optimal biomechanics during therapeutic exercises,
functional tasks, and return-to-sport activities. Optimal biomechanics, which also may be
specific to the individual, may enhance tissue healing and optimize performance.

Obtain equipment necessary during postoperative phase.
Mobility and daily tasks
Positioning during sitting, standing, and lying to maximize comfort and minimize stress to
healing tissues
Safe performance of basic mobility tasks, such as getting in and out of bed, sitting to and
from standing, gait, stairs, and getting in and out of a car
Heel-to-toe gait pattern: Patients can maintain a weight-bearing limitation while using a
heel-to-toe pattern and, therefore, should avoid walking with the hip and knee held in
flexion to maintain toe-touch weight bearing. Walking with the hip and knee held in flexion
may increase stresses at the hip joint because of the muscle activation required to maintain
that pattern.
Correction of noted movement impairments, such as excessive hip adduction or pelvic
tilting, during mobility tasks
Therapeutic exercises
Exercises should be provided to minimize the effects of immobilization and gently
strengthen muscle while maintaining precautions.

Range of motion exercises should not be too aggressive in this early phase.
Active straight-leg raises should not be performed. Active straight-leg raises may result in
increased forces in the anterior hip joint,48 which may place considerable stress on the
anterior hip joint structures, such as the labrum, the capsule, and the iliopsoas muscle.
Straight-leg raise also may place increased stress on the lumbar spine in patients with
inadequate abdominal control.
In addition to strengthening the major muscle groups, the intrinsic/short hip rotators also
should be strengthened because they are believed to provide hip joint stability.49-51
Aquatic exercise (after adequate incision healing) or upright bicycling (with uninvolved limb
only) can be used for cardiovascular endurance.
Emphasis should be placed on movement quality during performance of all exercises.
Cues to use abdominal muscles to stabilize the pelvis during exercises involving the lower
extremities should be given.
Palpation may be used to ensure appropriate muscles are activated during specific
exercises.
Strengthening and flexibility exercises for the uninvolved limb, trunk, and upper extremities
can be used.

Phase 4: Return to Sports Activity
Patients in the return-to-sport phase have full–weight-bearing status and no precautions
in place. This phase of management may occur between 14 and 24 weeks
postoperatively, depending on the tissues affected by the surgical procedure and the
patient’s response to treatment.
Various functional tests are available. The validity of these tests is controversial;
however, each test may offer some insight on how the patient may perform in specific
sports activities. A battery of tests should be used to assess balance, coordination,
agility, strength, and movement pattern. Common functional tests include the following:
Limb symmetry index: goal to reach greater than 85%
Double-limb performance tests
Modified agility T-test
Modified pro shuttle test
Modified long shuttle test
Single-limb performance tests
Hop tests
Single hop for distance
Cross-over hop for distance
Triple hop for distance
Six-meter timed hop
Lateral step test
Sport/position-specific functional tests
In addition to variables assessed, such as time and distance, the patient’s movement
quality should be assessed, and any noted impairments should be addressed.
